newsitem.title: ALBANIA: New Albanian president is newcomer to politics.
newsitem.headline: New Albanian president is newcomer to politics.

text.p: Rexhep Mejdani, a bespectacled physicist whose idol is Albert Einstein, was elected president of Albania on Thursday after only a year in politics.
His Socialists and their allies won a landslide victory in June 29 general elections, ousting the Democratic Party of his predecessor Sali Berisha from power after five years.
Unlike Berisha and Socialist leader Fatos Nano, Mejdani says proudly that he was never a member of the once all-powerful communist party and nor were his brothers or sisters.
He was elected Socialist secretary general at a reformist congress last August and became the party's central figure while Nano was in jail on corruption charges.

Mejdani, a tall, lean chainsmoker who is credited with keeping its feuding factions in check, said he would resign from the party and is expected to move to the presidential palace on a hillside outside Tirana.
"I call on all Albanians to help me realise my mission on the difficult road of normalising the life of the country and its institutions," he said.
"I call on all Albanian immigrants wherever they are to come back and contribute to the reconstruction of Albania."
Mejdani became a member of an emergency presidential council soon after communism was toppled in Albania in 1990 and was chosen chairman of the election commission.
"My character drives me to join the side of those who are in a difficult position and need me," he said in an early interview.
Last month's elections, prepared by a Socialist-led national unity government, were held as part of a deal which Mejdani and other opposition leaders negotiated with Berisha in March.

Mejdani campaigned with the slogan "We are against a king-like president and a president-like king", reflecting Socialist plans to give more powers to the prime minister and to reduce those of the head of state which grew dramatically under Berisha.
Most analysts believe Mejdani and Nano, the prime minister-designate, will be on the same wavelength but predict some friction.
"Mejdani finds it very difficult to change his mind once he is convinced he is right," said a senior Socialist who credits Mejdani with teaching the party to embrace pragmatism.

The Socialists, reformed heirs to the communists who ruled the country with an iron hand for four decades, also say he has brought the party closer to former political prisoners whom the communists persecuted.
He is expected to name a former anti-communist dissident who suffered long jail terms under the Stalinist dictatorship, as the presidency's secretary general.
Mejdani was born on August 17, 1944, the son of an officer in King Zog's army and a teacher mother.
He graduated from the University of Tirana in 1973, received a doctor's degree in quantum physics from the University of Paris three years later and returned to teach physics in Tirana University.
From 1991 until 1996, he devoted himself entirely to physics, publishing 51 research studies in foreign journals.
"I do not know myself how I got involved in politics. I have always felt much better in my laboratory," he told journalists when civil violence erupted in February.
"I would be happy with a deputy's seat so that I can get back to my students and resume the work I have abandoned for six months," he confided to a fellow Socialist before the elections.
Mejdani speaks French, English, Russian, Italian and German and enjoys the work of such writers as Stefan Zweig, Emile Zola, Jean Paul Sartre, Albert Camus and Fyodor Dostoevsky.
He is married to Lydka, a 43-year-old mathematician and they have an 18-year-old son and a 16-year-old daughter.
